questions.stem: Which statement describes a closed chemical system?
options: Energy can be exchanged with the surroundings, but matter cannot
Neither matter nor energy can be exchanged with the surroundings
Matter can be exchanged with the surroundings, but energy cannot
Both matter and energy can pass freely to and from the surroundings
questions.explanation: A closed system lets energy, such as heat, pass through its walls but keeps all the matter inside. A system that allows both matter and energy to cross is open, and one that exchanges neither is isolated.

questions.stem: An opened bottle of soft drink slowly goes flat, while a sealed bottle stays fizzy for months. Which explanation is best?
options: The sealed bottle is an isolated system, so neither heat nor gas can enter or leave it
The open bottle lets CO₂ gas escape, so equilibrium between dissolved and gaseous CO₂ is never reached
In the sealed bottle the dissolving of CO₂ has stopped completely, so no gas at all leaves the solution
Opening the bottle lowers its temperature, so CO₂ becomes much less soluble in the drink
questions.explanation: Equilibrium can only be reached in a closed system. In the open bottle, CO₂ that leaves the solution escapes, so the reverse change cannot keep pace and the drink goes flat. In the sealed bottle, dissolving and escaping continue at equal rates, which is dynamic, not stopped.

questions.stem: Which is an example of a physical equilibrium?
options: Liquid water and water vapour in a sealed flask at constant temperature
Nitrogen and hydrogen reacting to form ammonia in a sealed steel vessel
Ethanoic acid molecules partly ionising in an aqueous solution
Iron(III) and thiocyanate ions forming a red complex in solution
questions.explanation: Evaporation and condensation are physical changes, so the water and vapour system is a physical equilibrium. The other three involve new substances forming, so they are chemical equilibria.

questions.stem: Which statement is true of a reaction at dynamic equilibrium?
options: The forward and reverse reactions have both stopped completely
The concentrations of reactants and products are equal
The forward reaction is faster than the reverse reaction
The forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates
questions.explanation: At equilibrium both reactions keep going, but at the same rate, so concentrations stay constant. Constant does not mean equal: the reactant and product concentrations are usually different.

questions.stem: Brown NO₂ and colourless N₂O₄ are sealed in a flask: N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g). Which observation shows the system has reached equilibrium?
options: The pressure keeps falling at a steady rate
The intensity of the brown colour stays constant
The mixture becomes completely colourless
The brown colour darkens at a steady rate over time
questions.explanation: At equilibrium the concentrations no longer change, so macroscopic properties such as colour and pressure become constant. A colour or pressure that is still changing shows the forward and reverse rates are not yet equal.

questions.stem: A sealed flask initially contains only H₂(g) and I₂(g), which react: H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g). How do the rates change from the start until equilibrium?
options: The forward rate falls and the reverse rate rises until they are equal
The forward rate rises and the reverse rate falls until they are equal
The forward rate falls to zero while the reverse rate rises steadily
Both rates rise steadily from zero until they become equal
questions.explanation: As H₂ and I₂ are used up, their collisions become less frequent, so the forward rate falls. As HI builds up from zero, the reverse rate rises. Equilibrium is reached when the two rates are equal; neither drops to zero.

questions.stem: A small amount of radioactive iodine, I₂, is added to a sealed equilibrium mixture of H₂, I₂ and HI. Later, radioactivity is detected in the HI as well. What does this show?
options: Both the forward and reverse reactions continue at equilibrium
The equilibrium position has moved permanently to the right
The value of the equilibrium constant has increased
The radioactive iodine catalyses only the forward reaction
questions.explanation: The labelled iodine atoms can only end up in HI if I₂ is still reacting, and HI is also still breaking down. This is direct evidence that equilibrium is dynamic. Adding a little extra I₂ does shift the position slightly, but that would not explain labelled atoms moving between species.

questions.stem: The position of an equilibrium is said to lie far to the right. What does this mean?
options: The reaction reaches equilibrium very quickly once it starts
The forward reaction releases a large amount of heat energy
Products predominate over reactants in the equilibrium mixture
The forward reaction is faster than the reverse at equilibrium
questions.explanation: The position of equilibrium describes the relative amounts of reactants and products once equilibrium is reached. Lying to the right means mostly products. At equilibrium the forward and reverse rates are always equal, wherever the position lies.

questions.stem: An energy profile for a reversible reaction shows a forward activation energy of 80 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔH = −50 kJ mol⁻¹. What is the activation energy of the reverse reaction?
options: 30 kJ mol⁻¹
80 kJ mol⁻¹
50 kJ mol⁻¹
130 kJ mol⁻¹
questions.explanation: The products sit 50 kJ mol⁻¹ below the reactants, so the climb from products to the same transition state is 80 + 50 = 130 kJ mol⁻¹. Subtracting gives 30 kJ mol⁻¹, which would be right only if the reaction were endothermic.

questions.stem: Methane burns in oxygen, but CO₂ and water do not react back to form methane under ordinary conditions. Why is the reaction effectively irreversible?
options: The products have a higher enthalpy than the reactants, so the reverse reaction releases too much energy
The forward reaction has no activation energy, so it happens before the reverse reaction can start
Water and carbon dioxide are both covalent molecules, so they cannot collide with enough energy
The reverse reaction has a very large activation energy because the forward reaction is strongly exothermic
questions.explanation: For an exothermic reaction the reverse activation energy equals the forward activation energy plus the size of ΔH. Combustion releases a great deal of energy, so the reverse barrier is so high that almost no collisions overcome it. The products of combustion are lower, not higher, in enthalpy.

questions.stem: A reversible reaction has a forward activation energy of 60 kJ mol⁻¹ and a reverse activation energy of 100 kJ mol⁻¹. The temperature of the equilibrium mixture is lowered. What happens?
options: The reverse rate falls by a larger proportion, so the position shifts right
The forward rate falls by a larger proportion, so the position shifts left
Both rates fall by the same proportion, so the position does not change
The reverse rate rises while the forward rate falls, so it shifts left
questions.explanation: The forward reaction is exothermic (ΔH = 60 − 100 = −40 kJ mol⁻¹). Cooling reduces the fraction of collisions that can overcome a barrier, and the higher barrier is affected more, so the reverse rate drops more and the system shifts right. This agrees with Le Chatelier's principle: cooling favours the exothermic direction.

questions.stem: The forward reaction of an equilibrium is exothermic. What is the effect of raising the temperature?
options: The position shifts right and the value of K increases
The position shifts left, but K stays the same
The position shifts right, but K stays the same
The position shifts left and the value of K decreases
questions.explanation: Raising the temperature favours the endothermic direction, which here is the reverse reaction, so the position shifts left. Because temperature is the only factor that changes K, the value of K falls as products are converted back to reactants.

questions.stem: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), ΔH = −92 kJ mol⁻¹. The temperature of the equilibrium mixture is raised. Which explanation in terms of rates is correct?
options: Only the reverse rate increases, while the forward rate decreases, so the system shifts left
Both rates increase by the same proportion, so the equilibrium position does not change
The exothermic forward rate increases more than the reverse rate, so more ammonia forms
Both rates increase, but the endothermic reverse rate increases more, so the system shifts left
questions.explanation: Heating speeds up both reactions, because more collisions have enough energy. The reaction with the higher activation energy, the endothermic reverse reaction here, gains proportionally more, so it is faster until a new equilibrium is reached with less ammonia. The forward rate does not decrease when the temperature rises.

questions.stem: A sealed tube of N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g) turns a darker brown when it is placed in hot water. NO₂ is brown and N₂O₄ is colourless. What does this show?
options: The forward reaction is endothermic
The forward reaction is exothermic
Heating catalyses the forward reaction
K for this reaction does not depend on temperature
questions.explanation: The darker colour means more NO₂ at the higher temperature, so heating shifted the position to the right. Heating favours the endothermic direction, so the forward reaction must be endothermic. K does change with temperature; here it increases.

questions.stem: The equilibrium constant for a reaction is 0.5 at 300 °C and 4.0 at 500 °C. What can be concluded?
options: The reaction is faster at 300 °C than at 500 °C
The forward reaction is endothermic
The forward reaction is exothermic
A catalyst is present only at 500 °C
questions.explanation: K is larger at the higher temperature, so heating shifts the position towards products. Heating favours the endothermic direction, so the forward reaction is endothermic. A catalyst never changes K, and reactions are faster at higher temperatures, not lower.

questions.stem: Fe³⁺(aq) + SCN⁻(aq) ⇌ FeSCN²⁺(aq). Fe³⁺ is pale yellow and FeSCN²⁺ is deep red. A few drops of concentrated iron(III) nitrate solution are added to the equilibrium mixture. What is observed?
options: The red colour fades, as the reverse rate increases
The colour does not change, because K is constant
The solution turns colourless as SCN⁻ is used up
The red colour deepens, as the forward rate increases
questions.explanation: Adding Fe³⁺ makes collisions between Fe³⁺ and SCN⁻ more frequent, so the forward rate rises above the reverse rate and more red FeSCN²⁺ forms. K stays constant, but the system shifts to restore the equilibrium ratio.

questions.stem: Sodium hydroxide solution is added to the red equilibrium Fe³⁺(aq) + SCN⁻(aq) ⇌ FeSCN²⁺(aq), and a brown precipitate of Fe(OH)₃ forms. What happens to the red colour, and why?
options: It fades, because OH⁻ ions remove SCN⁻ and the reverse rate decreases
It deepens, because removing Fe³⁺ lowers the reverse rate and it shifts right
It fades, because removing Fe³⁺ lowers the forward rate and the system shifts left
It deepens, because OH⁻ ions collide with SCN⁻ and increase the forward rate
questions.explanation: The precipitate removes Fe³⁺ from solution, so Fe³⁺ and SCN⁻ collide less often and the forward rate drops below the reverse rate. FeSCN²⁺ breaks down faster than it forms, so the red colour fades. OH⁻ removes iron ions, not thiocyanate ions.

questions.stem: Extra SCN⁻ is added to the equilibrium Fe³⁺(aq) + SCN⁻(aq) ⇌ FeSCN²⁺(aq). How do the forward and reverse rates change from that moment?
options: The reverse rate falls at once; the forward rate stays the same until the rates are equal again
Both rates jump up at once by the same factor, so the equilibrium position does not change
The forward rate jumps up at once and then stays higher than the reverse rate from then on
The forward rate jumps up at once; the reverse rate then rises gradually until the rates are equal
questions.explanation: Adding SCN⁻ raises the frequency of forward collisions immediately, while the reverse rate depends only on [FeSCN²⁺], which has not yet changed. As FeSCN²⁺ builds up the reverse rate rises, and as reactants are used the forward rate eases, until they are equal again at a new equilibrium.

questions.stem: Water is added to the equilibrium mixture Fe³⁺(aq) + SCN⁻(aq) ⇌ FeSCN²⁺(aq), doubling its volume. Which way does the equilibrium position shift?
options: Right, towards the side with fewer particles in solution
It does not shift, because water is not in the equation
Right, because the water dilutes the red product only
Left, towards the side with more particles in solution
questions.explanation: Dilution lowers every concentration, and collisions between two reactant ions fall off more than the break-up of single FeSCN²⁺ ions. The system partly opposes the change by producing more dissolved particles, so it shifts left. Water need not appear in the equation for dilution to have an effect.

questions.stem: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g). The volume of the container is halved at constant temperature. Which way does the position shift?
options: It does not shift, because K is unchanged
Left, because the higher pressure favours reactants
Right, towards the side with fewer gas particles
Left, towards the side with more gas particles
questions.explanation: Halving the volume doubles every partial pressure. The system partly opposes this by shifting to the side with fewer gas particles, 2 mol on the right compared with 4 mol on the left, so more ammonia forms. K is unchanged, but the position still shifts.

questions.stem: The volume of a sealed container holding H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g) at equilibrium is halved at constant temperature. I₂ is purple; H₂ and HI are colourless. Which statement is correct?
options: The position shifts right, so the purple colour becomes much paler
The position shifts left, so the purple colour becomes more intense
The position shifts right, because the total pressure has doubled
The position does not shift, but the purple colour becomes more intense
questions.explanation: There are 2 mol of gas on each side, so changing the volume favours neither direction. The colour still deepens because the same amount of I₂ is now packed into half the volume, doubling its concentration.

questions.stem: Argon gas is pumped into a rigid container holding N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) at equilibrium, at constant temperature. What happens to the equilibrium?
options: It shifts right, because argon raises the collision frequency of nitrogen and hydrogen
It does not shift, because the partial pressures of the reacting gases are unchanged
It shifts right, because the total pressure has increased and fewer gas particles are favoured
It shifts left, because argon particles collide with ammonia and break it down faster
questions.explanation: In a rigid container the volume is fixed, so adding an unreactive gas does not change the concentration or partial pressure of N₂, H₂ or NH₃. The forward and reverse rates are unaffected, so there is no shift even though the total pressure rises.

questions.stem: Extra N₂ is added to N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) at equilibrium, at constant volume and temperature. Compared with the original equilibrium, which is true at the new equilibrium?
options: All three concentrations are the same as before
[N₂] and [NH₃] are both higher, and [H₂] is lower
[N₂] is back to its original value, and [NH₃] is higher
[N₂] and [H₂] are both lower, and [NH₃] is higher
questions.explanation: The system shifts right, using up some of the added N₂ along with H₂ and forming NH₃. It only partly opposes the change, so [N₂] stays above its original value, [H₂] ends lower and [NH₃] ends higher.

questions.stem: What is the effect of adding a catalyst to a reaction mixture at equilibrium?
options: The position shifts right, but the value of K is unchanged
The position shifts left and K decreases
Neither the position of equilibrium nor K changes
The position shifts right and K increases
questions.explanation: A catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally, so an equilibrium mixture stays as it is. Its use is to reach equilibrium sooner, not to change the yield.

questions.stem: Why does a catalyst not change the position of an equilibrium?
options: It is used up by the forward reaction and then regenerated by the reverse reaction
It lowers the activation energies of the forward and reverse reactions by the same amount
It lowers the activation energy of the forward reaction but not of the reverse reaction
It increases the size of ΔH for the forward and reverse reactions by the same amount
questions.explanation: The catalysed pathway has a lower transition state, which lowers both barriers by the same amount, so both rates increase together. ΔH is unchanged, because the reactant and product energies are unaffected.

questions.stem: Which statement of Le Chatelier's principle is correct?
options: If a system at equilibrium is disturbed, it adjusts to partly oppose the change
If a system at equilibrium is disturbed, it adjusts to fully reverse the change
If a system at equilibrium is disturbed, K changes to cancel out the change
If a system at equilibrium is disturbed, it stops until the change is removed
questions.explanation: The system shifts in the direction that partly counteracts the disturbance, for example using up some added reactant. It never removes the change completely, and only a change of temperature alters K.

questions.stem: For 2NO₂(g) ⇌ N₂O₄(g), a concentration-time graph shows both concentrations jumping up suddenly at time t. After t, [NO₂] gradually falls and [N₂O₄] gradually rises. What change was made at time t?
options: A catalyst was added to the mixture
The volume of the container was decreased
More NO₂ was added to the container
The temperature of the mixture was increased
questions.explanation: Only a change in volume makes every concentration jump at the same instant. Compressing the gases favours the side with fewer particles, so NO₂ then falls and N₂O₄ rises. Adding NO₂ alone would make only [NO₂] jump, and a temperature change causes gradual changes with no jump.

questions.stem: For the exothermic reaction 2NO₂(g) ⇌ N₂O₄(g), a graph shows that at time t, with no sudden jump, [NO₂] begins to rise gradually and [N₂O₄] begins to fall gradually to new constant values. What change was made at time t?
options: Some N₂O₄ was removed from the mixture
The temperature was increased
The temperature was decreased
The container volume was increased
questions.explanation: A temperature change shifts the position without an instant jump in any concentration. Moving towards NO₂ is the endothermic direction, which heating favours. Changing the volume or removing N₂O₄ would show a sudden step in the graph at time t.

questions.stem: Orange Cr₂O₇²⁻ and yellow CrO₄²⁻ are in equilibrium: Cr₂O₇²⁻(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ 2CrO₄²⁻(aq) + 2H⁺(aq). Sodium hydroxide solution is added. What colour change is seen, and why?
options: It turns yellow, because OH⁻ removes H⁺ and the system shifts right
It turns orange, because OH⁻ removes H⁺ and the system shifts left
It turns yellow, because OH⁻ reacts directly with the Cr₂O₇²⁻ ions
It turns orange, because the added water shifts the system to the left
questions.explanation: Hydroxide ions neutralise hydrogen ions, lowering [H⁺]. The reverse rate falls, so the system shifts right to replace some H⁺, forming more yellow chromate. Adding acid instead would turn the solution orange.

questions.stem: What is the equilibrium law expression for N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g)?
options: K = [NH₃] / ([N₂][H₂])
K = ([N₂][H₂]³) / [NH₃]²
K = [NH₃]² / ([N₂][H₂]³)
questions.explanation: Products go on top and reactants underneath, each concentration raised to the power of its coefficient in the balanced equation. Coefficients are powers, not multipliers.

questions.stem: What is the equilibrium law expression for CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g)?
options: K = [CaO][CO₂] / [CaCO₃]
K = [CaCO₃] / ([CaO][CO₂])
K = 1 / [CO₂]
K = [CO₂]
questions.explanation: This is a heterogeneous equilibrium. Pure solids have a constant concentration, so they are left out of the expression, leaving only the gas.

questions.stem: What is the equilibrium law expression for Cr₂O₇²⁻(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ 2CrO₄²⁻(aq) + 2H⁺(aq)?
options: K = [CrO₄²⁻][H⁺] / [Cr₂O₇²⁻]
K = [Cr₂O₇²⁻] / ([CrO₄²⁻]²[H⁺]²)
K = [CrO₄²⁻]²[H⁺]² / [Cr₂O₇²⁻]
K = [CrO₄²⁻]²[H⁺]² / ([Cr₂O₇²⁻][H₂O])
questions.explanation: Water is the solvent and its concentration is effectively constant, so it is left out, just like a pure solid. Each remaining concentration is raised to the power of its coefficient.

questions.stem: Which of these is a heterogeneous equilibrium?
options: CH₄(g) + H₂O(g) ⇌ CO(g) + 3H₂(g)
C(s) + H₂O(g) ⇌ CO(g) + H₂(g)
2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g)
N₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2NO(g)
questions.explanation: A heterogeneous equilibrium involves species in more than one phase, here solid carbon with gases. The others are all gases, so they are homogeneous.

questions.stem: At 25 °C, the equilibrium constant for a reaction is 1 × 10¹⁵. What does this indicate?
options: The equilibrium mixture contains mostly products
The reaction reaches equilibrium extremely quickly
The equilibrium mixture contains mostly reactants
The forward reaction has a very low activation energy
questions.explanation: A very large K means the products term in the expression greatly outweighs the reactants, so the reaction goes almost to completion. K says nothing about how fast equilibrium is reached.

questions.stem: Four reactions are compared at the same temperature. Which value of K shows the greatest extent of reaction?
questions.explanation: The larger the equilibrium constant, the further the position lies towards products. A K much smaller than 1, such as 2 × 10⁻⁸, means reactants predominate.

questions.stem: For the exothermic reaction 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g), which change alters the value of K?
options: Raising the temperature
Adding more oxygen to the mixture
Halving the volume
Adding a catalyst
questions.explanation: At a given temperature K is fixed. Changing concentrations or volume shifts the position until the same K is restored, and a catalyst has no effect on it. Raising the temperature favours the endothermic reverse reaction and lowers K.

questions.stem: Rising CO₂ in the atmosphere reduces the formation of calcium carbonate shells in seawater. Which explanation is correct?
options: Extra CO₂ raises the pH of the seawater, so the shells become less soluble and grow slowly
Dissolved CO₂ reacts with Ca²⁺ to form insoluble calcium hydrogencarbonate in the water
Extra CO₂ shifts Ca²⁺ + CO₃²⁻ ⇌ CaCO₃ to the right, so all the calcium is used up
Extra H⁺ from dissolved CO₂ converts CO₃²⁻ to HCO₃⁻, leaving less CO₃²⁻ to form CaCO₃
questions.explanation: Dissolved CO₂ forms carbonic acid, which ionises to give H⁺. These ions react with carbonate ions to form hydrogencarbonate ions, lowering [CO₃²⁻], which organisms need to build CaCO₃. The pH falls, not rises, and calcium hydrogencarbonate is soluble.

questions.stem: In seawater, Ca²⁺(aq) + CO₃²⁻(aq) ⇌ CaCO₃(s). If the carbonate ion concentration falls, what happens?
options: The position shifts right, so more calcium carbonate precipitates
The position does not shift, because CaCO₃ is a solid
The position shifts left, but only if a catalyst is present
The position shifts left, so calcium carbonate tends to dissolve
questions.explanation: Lowering [CO₃²⁻] slows the forward reaction, so the system shifts left and solid calcium carbonate tends to dissolve. That is why ocean acidification harms shells and coral skeletons. The solid is left out of the expression, but the equilibrium still responds to the ions in solution.
